title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from a single hosted LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The design used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused across both arms) and allowed up to one validator‑triggered repair in the guarded arm. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial) using the declared model gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms: baseline safe = 240/240, guarded safe = 240/240. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract the guarded arm could only change the paired outcome if the shared initial candidate failed validation or if the validator invoked a repair; in this run the shared candidates passed validation and no repairs were invoked, producing a degenerate paired contrast. We present the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, quantitative analysis, an evidence‑based explanation for the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Automating translation of high‑level operator intent into multi‑device network configurations is a core NetOps objective. Recent work positions large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows as capable configuration planners, but textual correctness metrics fail to capture ordering, dependency, and invariants required for safe application in live networks. Emulation‑grounded, closed‑loop evaluation—where generated configurations are executed in device/simulator environments and deterministically scored—reveals semantic failure modes (ordering mistakes, transient violations, protected‑resource touches) not visible in text‑only tests [1].

A common architectural approach is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM proposes a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants, and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations are detected [2,3]. GVR has shown promise for syntactic and many semantic faults, but open empirical questions remain about verifier benefit under distribution shift and adversarial prompts and about experimental designs that yield informative paired contrasts between guarded and unguarded pipelines. This paper reports a fully preregistered paired experiment that measures a single estimand—the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline)—executed under shared_initial_candidate semantics. We preserve and reference archived execution and analysis artifacts and focus on explaining the observed (degenerate) paired outcome and on recommendations to make future paired GVR tests informative.
sections.related_work:
Executable NetOps benchmarks and emulation frameworks have recently been developed to expose workflow and planning faults for LLM agents rather than only assessing textual fidelity; NetConfArena is one example [1]. Research on automatic configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and demonstrates that deterministic validators can enable high repair coverage for many benchmarked faults, though semantic coverage depends on verifier design [2,4]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising patterns for operational NetOps automation and safety [3,5]. Engineering precedent from configuration analysis tooling (e.g., Batfish) illustrates incremental verification design and verifier engineering tradeoffs [6].

Our study differs from prior work by combining (a) a predeclared paired estimand, (b) preregistered shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, (c) emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring, and (d) archival per‑call traces and validator traces that permit exact reconciliation from preregistered estimand to archived analysis outputs.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied; safe_apply = 0 indicates no such violation. Analysis used a paired binary executor producing a paired contingency table, exact McNemar two‑sided test, and bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples).

Design and sampling: The design was paired with shared_initial_candidate generation semantics: the adapter produced exactly one initial LLM generation per task and both arms used that same candidate. N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks were deterministically generated and blocked into topology/vendor clusters: in‑distribution 60% (144 tasks), distribution‑shift 20% (48 tasks), adversarial prompt 20% (48 tasks). Adversarial prompts were generated under a fixed, preregistered adversary protocol. The guarded arm could request at most one validator‑triggered repair per task.

Model, verifier, and adapter contract: Execution declared model = gpt-5-mini and verifier = deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and enforced shared_initial_candidate semantics; therefore paired differences could only arise if the single shared candidate failed deterministic validation or if the guarded arm applied a repair. The adapter recorded per‑call metadata and provider audit counters.

Scoring, exclusions, and missingness: A deterministic emulator+validator scored each final configuration binary (safe vs unsafe). Predeclared exclusions: pairs flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) would be excluded from the primary analysis and handled in sensitivity analyses; infra failures after the preregistered retry policy would be excluded. Retry policy allowed up to two infra recovery attempts. All exclusion and missingness rules and counts were archived.

Statistical analysis: Primary analysis used the paired contingency table, an exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant pairs, and bootstrap percentile 95% confidence intervals (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Secondary planned analyses included median repair counts and total model calls per task. Multiplicity: single primary hypothesis; secondary tests to be FDR‑corrected when reported.
sections.results:
Execution summary and accounting: The run completed per the preregistered plan: planned episodes = 480, completed episodes = 480, complete pairs = 240. Provider audit recorded exactly one shared initial generation per task (hosted model call events = 240) and total model calls used = 240. No infra failures or preregistered exclusions occurred.

Primary binary outcomes: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Condition summary: baseline successes = 240, baseline failures = 0; guarded successes = 240, guarded failures = 0. Paired contingency: n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied (repair attempts = 0). Representative validator traces record parsed command counts, required_command_count and validator PASS semantics; in every task the shared initial candidate both satisfied the verifier checks and matched the guarded final configuration. Consequently, the guarded arm could not create discordant pairs under the adapter contract, yielding the degenerate paired contrast reported above.

Subgroup slices: In‑distribution, distribution‑shift, and adversarial subsets are all degenerate (zero unsafe applies in both arms); thus subgroup paired contrasts are also 0.00 with identical, degenerate CIs and no discordant pairs.
sections.discussion:
Mechanistic explanation for the null paired contrast: The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one shared LLM output per task that both arms evaluated; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 passed every shared candidate; and the guarded arm had no opportunity or need to call the repair routine. Under that contract the guarded arm can only affect the paired outcome when the shared candidate fails validation or when a repair is applied; neither occurred here. The degenerate outcome is therefore a design‑level consequence rather than evidence that verifiers are universally unnecessary.

Design tradeoffs and implications: Shared_initial_candidate semantics reduces model‑call budget and guarantees a direct pairing of LLM outputs, simplifying paired inference, but it also eliminates generator variability between arms and makes observed verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures. To obtain an informative paired estimate of a verifier’s causal effect researchers should (a) permit independent initial generations per arm or randomize generator draws across arms, (b) increase repair budgets (allow multiple repair iterations to exercise repair search), or (c) strengthen adversary protocols to create failure opportunities that validators can detect. These recommendations arise directly from the archived provider audit and validator traces that show identical shared responses and zero repairs.

Threats to validity: Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate contract is an explicit design choice that restricts causal contrast interpretation; this contract and its runtime adherence were enforced by the adapter. Construct validity: the deterministic verifier encodes a finite check set; passing the verifier does not prove absence of all semantic faults unmodeled by the verifier. External validity: tasks were drawn from a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; extrapolation to production, diverse vendor ecosystems, and operator workflows requires further empirical study. Conclusion validity: the realized baseline unsafe rate = 0 prevents detecting verifier benefit in this design—future power analyses must account for generator variability and stronger adversaries to induce informative discordant pairs.

Practical recommendations for future GVR evaluations: (1) If paired causal estimation is the goal, avoid shared_initial_candidate semantics or deliberately inject independent generator variability across arms. (2) Permit larger repair budgets and instrument repair traces to study repair search dynamics. (3) Expand adversary protocols beyond a single fixed seed to probe adaptive prompt manipulations. (4) Improve verifier semantic coverage and add cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator outcomes to detect potential false‑safe cases.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑generated network configurations. Observed outcome: all 240 paired tasks were safe under both baseline and guarded arms, yielding a paired difference of 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). This degenerate result is attributable to the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and the fact that no shared candidates failed deterministic validation; consequently, no repairs were invoked and the guarded arm could not create discordance. The archived artifacts and analysis support these conclusions and motivate concrete experimental changes (generation semantics, adversary strength, repair budget) required to produce informative paired contrasts in future studies.

disclosure_statement: Execution used the declared hosted model gpt-5-mini via the registered adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed under that frozen plan after the autonomy lock. The adapter enforced shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial LLM generation per task reused across both arms); under that contract paired divergences could only arise if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; all literature review, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock. Execution artifacts (preregistration, execution manifest, per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis outputs) are archived and available for inspection; the Disclosure does not reproduce per‑file provenance here. No manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier.
